description: Poaceae-only glossary extensions. Canonical shared definitions are fetched read-only from Hays-County-Botany. Existing credited grass photo URLs reused from the published Grass ID Lab; each image is illustrative and may not demonstrate every named microfeature.

panicle.plain: A branching flowerhead whose smaller flower-bearing branches come off a main axis.
panicle.where: Trace the inflorescence axis; look for side branches and then the spikelets they carry.
panicle.why: Distinguish a broad open panicle from a spike or narrow contracted panicle.

photo.label: Purple lovegrass — open branching flowerhead
photo.creator: David J. Stang
photo.note: A whole flowering panicle, not an isolated branch dissection.

stolon.plain: A stem that runs along the ground surface and can root at its joints.
stolon.where: Trace a runner on the soil surface and look for roots or shoots at nodes.
stolon.why: Do not confuse a surface stolon with an underground rhizome or a decumbent flowering culm.

photo.label: Bermudagrass — connected creeping stem and leafy nodes
photo.creator: Photographer credited as no rights reserved
photo.note: Creeping stem is visible; the original gallery does not establish whether it was above or below the soil.

internode.plain: The stretch of stem between two successive nodes (joints).
internode.where: Locate two nodes on one culm; the stem section connecting them is the internode.
internode.why: Internode length, shape and surface can be useful characters.

photo.label: Silky bluestem stem node
photo.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
photo.note: A node close-up; trace the internode on the specimen.

floret.plain: A single tiny grass flower, usually enclosed by a lemma and palea, inside a spikelet.
floret.where: Use a hand lens on an opened spikelet; separate whole spikelet from one floret.
floret.why: Counting florets per spikelet is critical in many grass groups.

photo.label: Blue grama — developing floral parts and spikelet details
photo.creator: Matt Lavin
photo.note: Developing reproductive parts; not an isolated complete mature floret.

rachilla.plain: The little central axis inside a grass spikelet that bears its florets.
rachilla.where: Dissect a multi-flowered spikelet and follow the tiny axis between florets.
rachilla.why: Rachilla hairs and articulation are useful diagnostic characters.

auricle.plain: A small ear-shaped projection at the base of a grass leaf blade beside the collar.
auricle.where: Spread the blade away from the sheath and inspect both sides at the junction.
auricle.why: Auricles may clasp the stem, be small or be absent; do not confuse them with the ligule.

midrib.plain: The central lengthwise vein of a leaf blade.
midrib.where: Hold the blade against light and inspect both faces along its center.
midrib.why: A pale midrib is not necessarily raised; observe color and relief separately.

photo.label: Variable panicgrass — broad leaf blade with visible parallel veins
photo.creator: Alex Abair
photo.note: Parallel veins are visible; this image does not demonstrate raised ribs or a raised midrib.

venation.plain: The arrangement of veins in a leaf; grasses commonly have mostly parallel veins.
venation.where: View the leaf blade in side light to compare the lengthwise veins.
venation.why: The number and prominence of veins can help distinguish grasses.

photo.label: Variable panicgrass — broad leaf blade with visible parallel veins
photo.creator: Alex Abair
photo.note: Parallel veins are visible; this image does not demonstrate raised ribs or a raised midrib.

raised-ribs.plain: Lengthwise ridges that project above the blade surface, often associated with veins.
raised-ribs.where: Look across the blade edge-on, then use side light or touch to detect ridges.
raised-ribs.why: Raised ribs differ from flat veins or color bands; the pictured leaf does not prove ribs.

leaf-blade.plain: The free, often flat or rolled part of a grass leaf extending beyond the sheath.
leaf-blade.where: Follow a leaf from its sheath to its free tip.
leaf-blade.why: Blade width, folding, hairs and veins are common field-identification clues.

photo.label: Variable panicgrass — broad leaf blade with visible parallel veins
photo.creator: Alex Abair
photo.note: Parallel veins are visible; this image does not demonstrate raised ribs or a raised midrib.

trichome.plain: A hair or hairlike outgrowth produced by a plant surface.
trichome.where: Inspect the leaf, sheath or culm with side light or a hand lens.
trichome.why: Hair placement, length and direction can be diagnostic.

photo.label: KR bluestem — collar region and hairs
photo.creator: Matt Lavin
photo.note: Collar hairs visible; do not infer all hairs are ligule cilia.

bristle.plain: A stiff slender projection; in bristlegrasses some bristles are modified sterile branchlets.
bristle.where: Inspect how each projection attaches; do not assume it is a lemma awn.
bristle.why: Bristles below a Setaria spikelet differ from awns arising from glumes or lemmas.

photo.label: Knotroot bristlegrass — reproductive units, bristles, feathery stigmas
photo.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
photo.note: Bristles and feathery stigmas are distinct structures; 3-mm source scale.

ciliate.plain: Bearing a fringe of hairs along an edge or margin.
ciliate.where: Look along the edge of a ligule, sheath or other structure with magnification.
ciliate.why: The position of edge hairs matters more than simply seeing a hairy plant.

photo.label: KR bluestem — collar region and hairs
photo.creator: Matt Lavin
photo.note: Collar hairs visible; do not infer all hairs are ligule cilia.

pedicel.plain: A short stalk supporting a single flower or spikelet.
pedicel.where: Look where a grass spikelet attaches to its flowering branch.
pedicel.why: Paired sessile and pedicelled spikelets are diagnostic in several bluestems.

photo.label: Silky bluestem — stalked spikelet beside scale
photo.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
photo.note: Detached reproductive unit; the pedicel's attachment is not shown.

stigma.plain: The pollen-receiving part of the pistil; grass stigmas are usually feathery.
stigma.where: Look for fine feathery parts protruding from flowering spikelets.
stigma.why: Feathery stigmas are not awns or bristles.

photo.label: Knotroot bristlegrass — reproductive units, bristles, feathery stigmas
photo.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
photo.note: Bristles and feathery stigmas are distinct structures; 3-mm source scale.

anther.plain: The pollen-producing part of a stamen.
anther.where: Look for small dangling pollen-bearing sacs emerging from florets.
anther.why: Dangling anthers can help distinguish actual flowering structures from awns.

gland.plain: A small structure that secretes substances, sometimes visible as a dot or sticky ring.
gland.where: Inspect nodes, leaf sheaths and the base of blades for dots or rings.
gland.why: A gland ring is different from a band of hairs or a simple swollen node.

sheath-margin.plain: The edge of a leaf sheath where the sheath wraps around the culm.
sheath-margin.where: Find the longitudinal opening or seam of the sheath and inspect its edges.
sheath-margin.why: Sheath margins can be open, overlapping or fused; check the actual collar region.

photo.label: KR bluestem — collar region and hairs
photo.creator: Matt Lavin
photo.note: Collar hairs visible; do not infer all hairs are ligule cilia.

flag-leaf.plain: The uppermost leaf beneath a grass inflorescence.
flag-leaf.where: Follow the flowering culm downward from its seedhead to the highest leaf.
flag-leaf.why: The flag leaf position can help orient close examination, but it is not present on all specimens.

decumbent.plain: Lying along the ground at the base but bending upward at the tips.
decumbent.where: Follow the actual culm from its base through the bend and toward the tip.
decumbent.why: A decumbent culm may root at nodes without being a true stolon.

photo.label: Bermudagrass — connected creeping stem and leafy nodes
photo.creator: Photographer credited as no rights reserved
photo.note: Creeping stem is visible; the original gallery does not establish whether it was above or below the soil.

geniculate.plain: Bent abruptly at a joint, like a knee.
geniculate.where: Inspect the culm at successive nodes for sharp changes in direction.
geniculate.why: Knee-bent growth differs from a long continuous surface runner.

photo.label: Silky bluestem stem node
photo.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
photo.note: A node close-up; trace the internode on the specimen.

scabrous.plain: Rough to the touch because of minute stiff projections.
scabrous.where: Gently stroke the blade edge or vein in both directions.
scabrous.why: Roughness can occur on specific margins, veins or sheaths, not every surface.

crown.plain: The concentrated basal region from which grass shoots and roots arise.
crown.where: Separate old leaves gently at the plant base and inspect where multiple culms originate.
crown.why: A hard crown should not automatically be recorded as a spreading rhizome.

culm-node.plain: The joint on a grass stem where a leaf sheath attaches.
culm-node.where: Follow the culm and locate the often swollen joint between internodes.
culm-node.why: Node hairs, rooting and gland rings are separate traits.

photo.label: Silky bluestem stem node
photo.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
photo.note: A node close-up; trace the internode on the specimen.

involucre-bristles.plain: Modified bristles surrounding one or more spikelets; in sandburs they become a spiny bur-like unit.
involucre-bristles.where: Inspect the base of the bur under magnification, rather than counting the spines as lemma awns.
involucre-bristles.why: These bristles are outside the spikelet and are distinct from glumes and lemmas.

photo.label: Knotroot bristlegrass — reproductive units, bristles, feathery stigmas
photo.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
photo.note: Bristles and feathery stigmas are distinct structures; 3-mm source scale.

rachis-branch.plain: A branch arising from the main inflorescence axis and carrying spikelets.
rachis-branch.where: Trace a flowering head from the main axis outward through its branches.
rachis-branch.why: Branch pattern helps separate panicles, spikes and racemose arrangements.

photo.label: Purple lovegrass — open branching flowerhead
photo.creator: David J. Stang
photo.note: A whole flowering panicle, not an isolated branch dissection.
